observations: Many single-domain globular proteins undergo a reversible, two-state reaction where N represents the biologically active native state, and U represents the unfolded state.
Typical globular proteins have Gibbs free energy of unfolding values of ∼7 kcal/mol at room temperature.
Only one out of 10^{5} protein molecules are not in the native state.
Different tools give similar thermodynamic values for protein stability.
NMR-detected HDX can be used to assess stability at the level of individual backbone amide protons for proteins up to about 200 residues.
When a proton is exchanged for a deuteron, its cross-peak volume decreases with time and finally disappears.
If HDX occurs on a time scale of minutes or longer, the exponential decay in the volume of each amide proton cross peak can be used to obtain a rate constant for exchange.
Under the EX1 limit, the exchange rate is rate-determining and is usually associated with less stable proteins or proteins at basic pH.
At the EX2 limit, exchange from the open state is rate-determining.
